newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Major airlines raise ex-HK air cargo rates to Europe.
newsitem.headline: Major airlines raise ex-HK air cargo rates to Europe.

text.p: Major airlines have raised their ex- Hong Kong air cargo rates on routes to Europe for the second time this year as they enjoy high demand for space in an Easter "mini-peak" season, airfreight industry sources told Reuters.

March, a traditionally busy month for the air cargo industry in the territory, has been living up to expectations following the long lay-off in China and Hong Kong's hinterland for the Chinese New Year holiday. Factory production is now back in full swing and exporters are vying for space.

With demand high, airlines have taken the opportunity to raise rates by between 70 Hong Kong cents and $1.50 per kg to most leading European destinations. Many carriers have also raised their rates to Hong Kong, sources said.

"Excellent -- I wish I had more space available" is how KLM's regional director sales for North Asia, Tom Presnail described the current Hong Kong market. He reported a 45 percent increase in tonnage from Hong Kong to KLM's Amsterdam hub and onto destinations on its worldwide network between last September and February.
There was also a 38 percent increase in freight tonnes kilometres, Presnail said from his Tokyo headquarters.

One example of how Asian exporters are keeping European airlines busy is continued demand for Sony 'PlayStation' computer games which have continued to sell after the Christmas rush in large quantities and are being airlifted by KLM from Tokyo.
Air France Cargo said it had too much cargo for its three weekly freighters in addition to six Combi flights from Hong Kong to Paris and was experiencing a small backlog.
Other cargo managers contacted were also pleased with business and said they were glad there had not been a repeat of last year when the market was memorably bad.

Some freight forwarders have found their profit margins squeezed and another rate rise drew criticism from the secretary of the Hong Kong Association of Freight Forwarding Agents (HAFFA). Bengt Sjoeberg, who is also an executive with freight forwarders ASG (HK) Ltd, complained about the airlines' "shortsightedness and short term opportunism."

"Our clients are getting tired and fed up. It puts forwarders in a very difficult position where many have to absorb the increase because we all know the current peak is only going to last for a short time and rates will come down again. Airlines putting rates up and down is not beneficial for the market and would much prefer a much more stable rate policy from carriers than what they have benn doing lately," Sjoeberg complained.
Another major freight forwarder said he had had to "grin and bear" the latest rise by absorbing some of the rate rise. Others said their customers were paying the price.

The vice-chairman of the Hong Kong Association of Freight Forwarding Agents and chairman of freight forwarding firm BALtrans Holdings Limited, Anthony Lau, said the freight forwarding industry was generally sympathetic to the airlines rate rise as they try to recover lost ground in the battle for yield. He said agents were passing on the rate rise to their customers and he expected airline to try to maintain their rate level even when demand dropped within the next few weeks.

Industry sources said Hong Kong's home base carrier Cathay Pacific and Lufthansa Cargo, which dominate air cargo into Frankfurt from Hong Kong, were the prime movers for the latest rate rise. Some rival airline managers had been reluctant to follow suit but eventually followed the market trend.

"There was great reluctance from some airlines who didn't want to follow suit with another rate rise so soon after the last one in January, but practically everyone jumped on the bandwagon and raised their prices," the source said.

The top selling price to major cargo destinations such as Frankfurt and London is reported to be up to HK$25 per kilo on carriers such as Cathay, Lufthansa and Air France Cargo. For on carriers offering indirect services such as Korean Airlines via Seoul or Singapore Airlines, rates were slightly lower.
Cathay Pacific Cargo's marketing and sales manager Ray Jewell said flights to Europe were "looking very good."

"It has been unusually strong since the peak started last September, apart from a slight slackening during Chinese New Year. We expected it to be strong but it has been more than that. Load factors are good in both directions," Jewell added.

Lufthansa Cargo, which along with its joint venture partner Cathay Pacific Cargo, operates the most important single non-Asian route for Hong Kong's imports and exports to Frankfurt, said it has had an "excellent" first quarter much above expectations and despite the poor German economy.
Lufthansa Cargo's managing director for China, Hong Kong and Taiwan, Christian Sedelmaier, said current demand was being driven by the 'just-in-time' concept and not consumer demand.

"We are getting some overflow from sea shipments which are coming to the airlines because of heavy demand. But disposable income is weakening and the consumer mood in Germany is not so optimistic," he said. Lufthansa Cargo also raised its ex Hong Kong cargo rates by HK$1 per kilo from March 1.

Kenny Tang, the newly appointed chief operating officer of the territory's only all-cargo carrier, AHK Air Hong Kong Ltd in which Cathay is the majority shareholder, also said he was happy with business.

"Demand has picked up very quickly after Chinese new year and we have experienced very strong growth in March. It seems that trend will continue until Easter when there may be slow down and will boom again through June and July. The outlook is good," Tang said.

HACTL's managing director Anthony Charter sounded a cautionary note when he said world markets appeared to be quite bouyant but the threat of interest rate rises in the USA because of the balance of payments deficit was a concern for Hong Kong.
Space to Middle Eastern destinations is also said to be tight with carriers preferring to concentrate on long haul loads to Europe. Selling rates were said to be as high as HK$16 per kilo.
Emirates reported a strong pick up in the market with high demand for space.

"Our loads are good and cargo yields are favourable too. Unlike last year, in March this year everyone seems comfortable with the loads they are seeing on board. Most carriers are full and we presume it will stay that way until the middle of April," Jackie Lau, the Dubai-based carrier's cargo manager in Hong Kong said.

As a sign of the strong market, various carriers have announced extra frequencies to Hong Kong, including Lufthansa Cargo from 10 to 11 freighters from Frankfurt as part of its joint venture with Cathay Pacific.

Air Hong Kong is also expected to add an additional frequency to Dubai, Brussels and Manchester. It currently operates four Boeing 747-200 frequencies a week but is enjoying high load factors of "at least 90 and 95 percent and quite a few times 100 percent loads."
AHK's Kenny Tang expects to increase services to Dubai, Brussels and Manchester to a maximum five frequencies a week by May because of strong demand.
Singapore Airlines has also increased capacity to Manchester with an additional service from Singapore.

Scandinavian Airlines System acknowledged as being one of the smaller European carriers, is to add a fifth weekly frequency to its Hong Kong-Copenhagen non-stop passenger schedule from April 4 because of increased demand.

"March has definitely been very, very good and we see this trend continuing into April. It is very positive," according to the airline's general manager for Hong Kong, Macau, South China, Taipei and the Philippines, Per Moller Jensen. Garments and textiles were the predominant goods being carried along with high value electronic goods, he said.

"One influence may be the economies of Scandinavia are doing very well with high consumer demand. Many importers seem to be willing to be pay the higher rate to get there by air rather than by boat. The time to market is getting shorter and shorter,"
SAS also has plans to increase its Hong Kong service to daily frequency, but not until after Hong Kong's new Chek Lap Kok airport opens next year.
Both airline cargo managers and freight forwarders predict rates will stay at the current relatively high level despite the traditional fall in demand expected in April after the Easter holiday.

Industry observers said the airlines considered the relatively quieter months of May, June and July critical to their year-end profit and loss figures and they are determined to maintain the current rate level for as long as possible even if, as expected, demand drops after the Easter peak.
KLM's Tom Presnail, along with other managers from rival airlines, said he would be striving to maintain current rate levels even when demand drops and there is over-capacity.

"I would love to say 'come hell or high water' rates will stay high but as long as the market stays fairly strong and demand doesn't weaken, I don't see any change in the position. The market seems to be getting stronger and stronger at the moment," he said. - Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 8982 Fax+5017
